title: Day of the Programmer
directAnswer: Find the 256th day of a given year and print it as dd.mm.yyyy. The 256th day is always in September; the only thing that moves it is February's length. Use the Julian leap rule (year % 4 == 0) for years up to 1917, the Gregorian rule (divisible by 400, or by 4 but not 100) from 1919 on, and treat 1918 specially because that February lost 13 days. The answer is 12.09 in a leap year, 13.09 in a common year, and 26.09 in 1918.

remember.pattern: Branch on the calendar, then closed-form the date
remember.formula:
if year == 1918: return "26.09.1918"
if year < 1918:  leap = (year % 4 == 0)                  # Julian
else:            leap = (year % 400 == 0) or (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0)  # Gregorian
return ("12" if leap else "13") + ".09." + str(year)
rules: **1918 is the transition year** and the trap: switching from Julian to Gregorian deleted 13 days that February, so the 256th day is **26.09.1918**. Hardcode it.
**Years ≤ 1917 use the Julian rule** — leap iff `year % 4 == 0`. The `% 100` and `% 400` exceptions do **not** exist yet.
**Years ≥ 1919 use the Gregorian rule** — leap iff divisible by 400, or divisible by 4 but not by 100.
The 256th day is **always in September** for normal years: Jan–Aug is 243 days common / 244 leap, so day 256 is the 13th or 12th of September.
Output is fixed-width `dd.mm.yyyy` — zero-pad day and month (`26.09.1918`), never `26.9.1918`.
whenToUse: Date / calendar arithmetic with calendar-system changes
A fixed day-of-year mapped to a concrete date
Leap-year reasoning where the rule depends on the era
A small set of regimes you can branch over in O(1)
antiSignals: Arbitrary date differences across many years → use a date library or epoch days
Time zones / hours / minutes involved → far beyond integer day counting
You must handle every historical calendar quirk → this problem only spans one transition
The day-of-year is an input that varies → loop over months instead of hardcoding September
remember.takeaway: Calendar problems are branch-then-count: pick the right leap rule for the era, remember the one-off transition year, then map the day-of-year to a date. Day of the Programmer collapses to three cases because the 256th day never leaves September.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can encode era-dependent leap-year rules correctly, remember the 1918 Julian-to-Gregorian transition that deleted 13 days, and format the result as a fixed-width date — careful branching, not algorithmic depth.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Applying the Gregorian % 100 / % 400 exceptions to pre-1918 (Julian) years, or forgetting 1918 entirely and printing 13.09.1918 instead of 26.09.1918.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Separate the three regimes out loud — Julian (≤1917), the 1918 transition, Gregorian (≥1919) — and explain why only February's length can shift the 256th day.

problemStatement:
Marie invented a calendar where the Day of the Programmer falls on the **256th day** of the year. Given a year `year` in the inclusive range 1700 to 2700, return the date of the 256th day in the format `dd.mm.yyyy`.

The country used the **Julian** calendar through 1917, then switched to the **Gregorian** calendar. The transition happened in **1918**, when the day after January 31 was February 14 — that year February had only 15 days.
constraints: Julian leap year (year ≤ 1917): year divisible by 4
Gregorian leap year (year ≥ 1919): divisible by 400, or divisible by 4 and not by 100
1918 is the transition year: February has 15 days
Output format is exactly dd.mm.yyyy with zero-padding
understanding: The 256th day of the year is what we want as a calendar date. Days January through August total 243 in a common year and 244 in a leap year, so the 256th day lands on September 13 or September 12 respectively. The 1918 transition removed 13 days from February, shifting that year's 256th day to September 26. Everything reduces to: which leap rule applies, and is this the transition year?

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which calendar applies to which years?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Julian for years up to and including 1917, Gregorian for 1919 and later. 1918 is the one-time transition year with a shortened February.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What exactly happened in 1918?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The day after 31 January 1918 was 14 February 1918 — 13 dates were skipped, so that February had only 15 days and the 256th day became 26.09.1918.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the Gregorian century rules apply to Julian years?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Under Julian, every year divisible by 4 is a leap year — the % 100 and % 400 exceptions are Gregorian-only. Mixing them up is the classic bug.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should the date be formatted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: dd.mm.yyyy with zero-padded day and month, e.g. 12.09.2016 and 26.09.1918.

examples.explanation: Gregorian, 2017 is not divisible by 4 → common year. Jan–Aug = 243 days, so day 256 is September 13.
Gregorian, 2016 divisible by 4 and not by 100 → leap. Jan–Aug = 244 days, so day 256 is September 12.
Transition year: February lost 13 days (only 15 days), so Jan–Aug = 230 days and day 256 is September 26.

approaches.name: Month Accumulation — Count Days Across Months
approaches.whenToMention: A clean, general baseline: build month lengths and walk forward until you hit day 256. Mention it to show the general technique before specialising.
hints: Build the 12 month lengths for this specific year, getting February right via the era's leap rule (and the 1918 special case).
Walk month by month, subtracting each month's length from a running 'remaining = 256' until remaining no longer exceeds the current month.
When the loop stops, `remaining` is the day-of-month and the current month index gives the month. Format as dd.mm.yyyy.
approaches.complexityReasoning: At most 12 months are scanned regardless of input, and a fixed-size array of month lengths is used — constant time and space.
approaches.explanation:
This version generalises to any day-of-year, not just 256, by walking the calendar.

**Building the month table.** The only month whose length varies is February. Decide it first: 15 days if `year == 1918`, otherwise 29 if the era's leap rule fires (Julian `% 4` for ≤ 1917, Gregorian `% 400 / % 4 / % 100` for ≥ 1919), otherwise 28. Plug that into the standard `[31, feb, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]`.

**Walking to the target day.** Start `remaining = 256`. For each month, if `remaining` is larger than that month's length, the target lies further on — subtract the month and move to the next. Stop the moment `remaining <= days[month]`: the target falls inside this month, and `remaining` is now the day number. This is the same logic a calendar library uses to convert a day-of-year into a date.

**Why it lands in September.** January through August sum to 243 (common), 244 (leap), or 230 (1918). In every case `remaining` after August is between 1 and 30, so the loop halts on the September entry — confirming the closed-form shortcut the optimal approach uses.

**Why mention it.** It is dependable and obviously correct, and it makes the September observation concrete rather than asserted. The optimal version simply skips the walk because we know the answer is always September.
approaches.insight: Converting a day-of-year to a date is 'subtract month lengths until the day fits'. Getting February right per era is the only hard part; the walk itself is mechanical.

dryRun.intro: February is 15 days this year. Subtract month lengths from remaining = 256 until it fits.

approaches.name: Direct Branch — September Closed Form (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The tight answer. Since the 256th day is always in September, skip the walk and branch straight to the day.
hints: You already know Jan–Aug = 243 (common) / 244 (leap), so day 256 is September 13 or 12 — no month walk needed.
Branch the leap decision by era: Julian (% 4) for ≤ 1917, Gregorian (% 400, % 4, % 100) for ≥ 1919.
Handle 1918 as a hardcoded 26.09.1918. Everything else is '12 or 13, dot 09, dot year'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A couple of comparisons and a string build — constant work, constant space, independent of the year.
approaches.explanation:
Since the target never leaves September, collapse the whole calendar into three printed strings.

**Why September is guaranteed.** January through August is `31+28+31+30+31+30+31+31 = 243` days in a common year and `244` in a leap year. Day 256 is therefore `256 − 243 = 13` (common) or `256 − 244 = 12` (leap) of September. In 1918, those eight months total `230` because February held only 15 days, so day 256 is `256 − 230 = 26` of September.

**The leap branch by era.** For years up to 1917 the calendar is Julian: a year is a leap year exactly when `year % 4 == 0`, with no century exceptions. For 1919 onward it is Gregorian: a leap year is divisible by 400, or divisible by 4 but not by 100. Applying the wrong rule near century boundaries (1800, 1900) is the most common silent error — under Julian, 1800 is a leap year; under Gregorian it would not be.

**The 1918 special case.** This single year is neither cleanly Julian nor Gregorian for our purposes — its February was truncated to 15 days. Hardcoding `26.09.1918` is clearer and safer than trying to fold it into the leap logic.

**Assembling the output.** Everything reduces to choosing `12` or `13` for the day, then appending `.09.` and the year. Zero-padding matters: the format is `dd.mm.yyyy`, so the month is always `09`, never `9`.
approaches.insight: The 256th day can only move when February's length moves, and February only touches the Jan–Aug prefix. That is why three printed strings cover every year in range — the rest is choosing the correct leap rule for the era.

edgeCases.behavior: Julian (≤ 1917): 1900 % 4 == 0 → leap → 12.09.1900. Under Gregorian it would be common — the era matters.
Gregorian: 2000 % 400 == 0 → leap → 12.09.2000. The 400-exception keeps it a leap year.

pitfalls: Forgetting 1918 entirely and printing 13.09.1918 instead of 26.09.1918.
Applying Gregorian century rules to years ≤ 1917 (e.g. wrongly calling 1900 common).
Dropping the zero-pad and printing 13.9.2017 instead of 13.09.2017.

commonMistakes: Using the Gregorian % 100 / % 400 exceptions for pre-1918 (Julian) years.
Forgetting the 1918 transition where February had only 15 days.
Outputting dates without zero-padding the day or month.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong leap rule for the era
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Before 1918 the calendar is Julian: every multiple of 4 is a leap year. Applying Gregorian century exceptions wrongly marks 1700, 1800, 1900 as common.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: boolean leap = year % 400 == 0 || (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0);  // wrong for year <= 1917

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the 1918 transition
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 1918 deleted 13 days from February, so the 256th day is 26.09, not the usual 13.09. Folding it into leap logic silently gets it wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
leap = year % 400 == 0 or (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0)
return f"{'12' if leap else '13'}.09.{year}"   # gives 13.09.1918

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unpadded date format
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The required format is dd.mm.yyyy. September must print as 09 and the day as two digits; 13.9.2017 fails the checker.
